utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know where it was exactly, do you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No, I don't even know now, to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked, and it was put to you that there were other places where the civilians blocked roads and that this was orchestrated. Can you quote any example where the civilians stopped passage for anyone, UNPROFOR, the BiH army, the HVO, or anyone?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Well, it was in Donji -- at Rijeka, on the lower road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the citizens organised by themselves?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, self-organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they orchestrated in any way?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any personal contacts with those people? Did you hear about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't. Thank you. One more question, if I may. You told us that you stopped UNPROFOR convoys bringing food. Would you try and think back and tell us whether you ever stopped any kind of vehicle or vehicles belonging to UNPROFOR, or any other international force or monitors, which was on the road alone, without taking food?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Grabovac, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded. You are free to go. We'll sit again at 2.40, when we'll hear from Mr. Nice about the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got some information to provide to the Chamber. Perhaps it would be preferable, given that it touches in part on things that are recently passed between us and Croatia, that if this five minutes was in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Zirdum.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: It is a pleasure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, would you please repeat your name, surname, place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: My name is Anto Zirdum. I was born in Pojara, the Derventa municipality in the Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was born on the 4th of June, 1956.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am also going to ask you, I see that you speak rather fast, as indeed I do, but please try and slow down a little bit and make pauses between question and answer to give the interpreters enough time to keep up with us, and this is very important for the record. You are a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have any children?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your education?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: University training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to university and graduate?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: In Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the Rijeka in Vitez or Rijeka in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: No, I mean Rijeka in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year did you serve?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: I did my service in Bileca and in Titograd. The reserve officer's school in Bileca, and then in Titograd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive a rank of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes. I received the rank of senior lieutenant. First of all, corporal, and then, by means of automatic procedure, lieutenant and second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you do now.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: I work in the organs of the central administration as an inspector in Central Bosnia for the social protection of displaced persons and on humanitarian issues as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. When did you move to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live before that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Before that, I lived and worked in Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: In Zenica. In fact, I grew up in Zenica and went to primary and secondary school there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then say that, as you yourself say, that you are a real Zenican, person from Zenica, who found a livelihood in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, I spent most of my life living in Zenica although I was born around Derventa, but I lived in Zenica and I have become accustomed to considering myself an inhabitant of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still have any close relatives near Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: My parents live in Zenica and so do my brothers. So my immediate family lives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, briefly, in which part of Zenica you live, what that area is called and where it is located in relation to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: It is the Travnica Street and the region towards Vitez in Travnik. It is on a hill which can be attained through Volovska Glava to Kuber and the road to Vitez and Busovaca if you were to go on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that that is the location of Mount Kuber which represents a natural boundary between Zenica and the Vitez region?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, as the highest peak and boundary, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your family, if I understood you correctly, it lives between Mount Kuber towards Zenica, in that region in between?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, at the foot of the mountain, closer to the foot of the mountain in the direction of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In Vitez, you have your wife and children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your nationality? You are a Croat, are you not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about your wife?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: My wife is a Muslim. She declares herself as a Croat of the Islamic faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when did you first report to the Territorial Defence in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Several days after the outbreak of the war, that is to say, after the events in Sarajevo, I heard a proclamation saying that all military-able men were to report to the Territorial Defence offices, and I think I was one of the first to report to one of their offices. I think that it was either in the municipality or in the SUP building. I can't remember where the office was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zirdum, what was your motive for reporting immediately?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: I considered it to be my civil duty as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina to respond to the proclamation sent out by the organs in power and authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I went to report immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to -- to your mind at that time, did you expect a possible aggression on the part of the JNA on Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, yes, the aggression had already started, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was your desire to contribute to the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, it was both my wish and my duty to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you reported, did anybody call you and mobilise you, assign you any duties? What happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Over the next ten days, I expected to be called up, that somebody would contact me in keeping with my military training and issue assignments, but that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Soon after that, the HVO became active. How did you experience the HVO at that time? What was the -- what did it represent, the HVO, to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: In the ten days that followed, I learned the HVO as being a general military and civilian organisation of the citizens regardless of -- separate from the parties. That is to say, I was informed that party affiliation was not important for participation and membership in the HVO but that it was the legitimate organisation of the Croatian people. I therefore considered that that was the right place for me to report to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your intention to report to them, was it once again based on the same motives that you had when you reported to the TO beforehand?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The defence of the country, you mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, the defence of the country from the Serbian aggression and the aggression of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zirdum, during that time, in that period -- but let me ask you, put the question to you this way: In your opinion, as somebody who attended events, what situation was the state in? How did it function? What about its organs of power and authority? Was it a state that functioned properly? Could you give us your opinions in a few words?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, I thought that the state functioned at the municipal level, but not at a higher administrative level. That is to say, it functioned poorly because power and authority was in Sarajevo, and they dealt with Sarajevo mostly and not the rest of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the previous set-up of the socialist Yugoslavia, Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, would it be fair to say that in the country's administration, that is to say, in organising the country's administrative bodies, the municipalities played a very significant role?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: The municipality or the socialist commune, as it was called then, did play a very important role, yes. It had a comprehensive role to play in local administration and local affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be true to say then, on the basis of what you have just said, that the municipality did succeed in performing its administrative functions whereas the central government did not? Could you describe the situation to us?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, the municipalities, yes, and there was some intermunicipality activity, that is to say, spontaneous agreements between neighbouring municipalities. At that level, it functioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try and illustrate this by quoting some examples. In 1992, was there the disintegration for the central organisation, for example, of the railways in Bosnia? Did they disintegrate or begin to disintegrate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. We've had a lot of evidence about these matters. Now, can we not move on, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber feels that it has had sufficient information on that subject, so let us continue and move on to points two and three. You said that you responded to the offer to join the HVO. You gave us your motives for doing so. What were your first assignments from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: My first assignment was to found the regional informative centre in Central Bosnia, and I was given the task of coordinator for technical matters, organisational and technical matters. That is to say, I was sent to organise work in this centre and then we went on to establishing radio and television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within the frameworks of that assignment, you were given the specific task of establishing radio and television Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true that, at that same time, Central Bosnia was undergoing an information blockade?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe this for us briefly.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Many transmitters had been taken over by the Yugoslav Serb army, the repeaters. Some of them were destroyed, others were controlled by the Serbs, and the repeater from Vlasic covered this area so we were in a total economic and information blockade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this blockade was imposed by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, because they had control of the transmitter Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, were there any different interests between the two most numerous, most populous people in the Lasva Valley, the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: No. At that time, their interests, their common interest was to defend themselves from the Serbian, or rather the Yugoslav aggressor, the Serb aggressor. And he was active in the Lasva Valley at Turbe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the television station was set up, what was your job in the television?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: When the television was established, I was a journalist. I had already become a journalist. So I did organisational work, but also worked as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what -- how you organised the television station in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, there was some kind of infrastructure in Pero Gudelj's building. He had some modest equipment, basic equipment. So that is something that we needed to start; you needed to have the equipment to start broadcasting. So we started building up the station with the help of the entrepreneur, Pero Gudelj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Pero Gudelj, who was he? In fact, was he the owner of the enterprise?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes. He was the owner of a large firm and he was the owner of a videotape and cable television, and he wanted to develop a commercial television station as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did this business undertaking, this joint venture with Mr. Gudelj turn out?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, we tried to evolve a programme which would have a dominant news broadcasting programme, and this programme would have special broadcasts and reports from the field. So we would go to Turbe and some other places where the Croats and Muslims joined forces in combating the Serbs. And I had a contact programme which was entitled "Open Talks," and I would invite guests to attend. Usually I would have two or three guests, it was a talk show. And there was usually one Croat and one Muslim taking part, and one Serb as well. We invested a great deal of effort in developing our programmes, but Mr. Pero Gudelj thought that the commercial aspect was more important. He wanted to see more advertisements rather than informative programmes, and this was a conflict of interest. We wanted to do programme work. He wanted to do advertising. So we didn't see eye to eye, and in a demonstrative way, I failed to accept this concept. I didn't want to prepare advertisements and programmes, and I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your other colleagues; did they stay or did they go?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: I think the day after I left, or perhaps a few days later, the professional journalists left. I think they did at least. But the technicians and the other staff stayed on for a time. I don't know what came of the television station after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: I went back to my own firm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: It was Vitezit, where I was head of the cadres department, personnel manager.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a question asked today about the Vitezit. Tell us about it. Vitezit was within the composition of the SPS factory.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: No. There were three companies: the SPS, Vitezit, and Sintevit. There were three actual companies functioning at that time, and they used to belong to an overall company that was called Unis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But for popular intents and purposes, for citizens in Vitez, when they refer to the factory, they call the factory under the general term of SPS.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, because it was the Slobodan Princip Seljo factory, the SPS, and later devolved into three separate companies. So this was a transformation; the SPS was divided into three sister companies later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regardless of the changes in organisation, all these companies were physically located in this large compound bordering on Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was called the SPS compound. That's what it was referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, how did you view the situation in 1992, the year we're talking about? When did you feel that there were greater political differences of opinion in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: This became obvious during the conflict in Novi Travnik, which means that it was at the beginning of October. In addition to my regular work, my regular job, I tried to rally intellectuals of the Lasva River Valley, especially the Croats and the Muslims, to try as citizens to react to the situation and to all the things that were not right in our midst.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just so that we can make things clear, would it be true to say that the HDZ and the SDA parties, in the elections that were held the previous year, that they were partners; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these two parties, in coalition, were victorious in the election, won the elections.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the period that you have just started describing to us, that is to say, late October, in your opinion, was that when this coalition began to disintegrate, or did this happen at another time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: At the time I was not a judge. I did not realise that it was the disintegration of the coalition; rather, I saw it as the resolution of outstanding issues with respect to the organisation and functioning of the society during those war days. It was only later that I was to realise that what had in fact happened was its disintegration. But what we thought at the time was that there were political disagreements between the political parties. That was quite normal, given the prevailing conditions, because both sides were brought into a situation where they had to contend with an aggression and they had to solve their problems as they went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A while ago you mentioned a forum of intellectuals of the Croats and Muslims in the Lasva Valley. Will you tell us in a few words, how did it come about?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: I told you that at the time I simply tried to prevail upon some intellectuals that we, as citizens, as intellectuals, as eminent citizens, should react to radicalism which began to be manifest in the policies of both the HDZ and the SDA, and to try to see that radicalism be brought down to some more moderate levels. With Suad Salkic, I discussed the matter, and he endorsed the idea. But I did the bulk of work. He is a very intelligent, a very nice man, but he's quite timid too, and he's not really ready to come forward. But whatever the case, we managed to arouse the interest of some 30 or 40 individuals; some 10 or 15 of them supported the idea of setting up that forum. However, it was very difficult to bring together more people. In point of fact, we used to gather in some small groups and discuss those issues on various occasions, and we were planning a large open forum, inviting intellectuals of all types and from all sides. Of course, it was very important to have there intellectuals from both parties, from the HDZ and SDA. I'm referring, of course, to the Vitez territory. When we organised that, some 20 or 25, or perhaps 30 people - I can't remember now what the whole was - they turned up. But the leading men of the SDA, the leading intellectuals in the SDA did not come, not one of them. And from the HDZ, only Mr. Ivan Santic and Mr. Pero Skopljak came. We taped it; however, it was taped badly and the sound was missing. But whatever the case, that was the only time that that forum met in a noteworthy number. After that it was concluded that it simply could not go on functioning unless it brought together also the leading men of the SDA, their intellectuals. Step by step it grew into a very informal group which fell short of its original objective, and it eventually simply withered away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to fill in a couple of voids that you left here. You said who was another mastermind of this; you said Suad Salkic. He's a Muslim, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, is it true that you aspired not to be a party, a political party, but just as your name indicated, a forum of intellectuals?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: We realised full well that we simply could not, and after all, we did not need to act in any other way except as eminent citizens, except as citizens of note who would draw the attention of the government to some excessive -- to phenomena of excesses, to things which were out of ordinary. I think it was after an incident which took place at the cemetery in Ahmici, that was the first serious incident between the HVO and the TO, and it was that, I think, which made us think about such a forum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the municipal government, I mean, the administration in the municipality, try in any way to prevent or to obstruct this forum?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you took part in yet another initiative, and the objective of that one was, I think, similar, wasn't it? What was that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, I was doing my job. But meanwhile, a private newspaper began to come out, Lasvanski Glasnik, the Lasva Herald. As a matter of fact, it had started before but now it had entered a new stage. It was my colleagues from the media centre, from the information centre, who worked there, and I tried to work together with them and do something, contribute there as an intellectual, as far as it was possible at that time. It was monthly, and I cooperated with them sometime between the second and the fourth issue. As a matter of fact, I think that the fourth issue never came out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was its editorial policy?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: It was a privately owned paper, and the editorial concept was to do what was otherwise impossible to do, that is, to cover this media space, to provide its citizens with only relevant political/social issues. Of course, since this was a private newspaper, it had to have advertisements and all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They came out sometime between late 1992 until about the eve of the conflict between the BH army and the HVO in April 1993; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Indeed. Its latest -- the last issue was to come out on the 16th. I suppose it was printed, but it was never collected; that is, somebody told me that he had seen a copy, that it had been printed. But I simply have no information as to what happened to it. I'd like to see that issue because it featured an interview I did with the chief of the police station in Vitez, Mr. Saban Mahmutovic, in Mahala. One could see what we talked about ten days before all that happened and what was the situation there, and that we were making interviews with both Muslims and Croats more or less on quite an equal footing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, we seem to be going too fast. I have to wait a little. But will you tell me, please, if that paper was biased in any way, either ethnically or politically, whether it favoured any one of the players there.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, the paper, yes, was "biased," if I may put it in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is why?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, it came out in the Croatian language. It's true that it was very poor Croatian language, but it is a fact that that is the language it was printed in. Otherwise, it maintained a complete balance, and it had among its contributors both Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For people who are not all that conversant with our language, perhaps we should explain it. At that time was there any Bosniak language in existence?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard about all of this. Let's move on to the relevant parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, what did you do on the 15th of April, 1993? What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, to me, it was a day just like any other, and I do not remember any particular details about it. As a matter of fact, a friend of mine from Zenica, who now lives in the Netherlands, his wife had come from the Netherlands, and he came to me -- he came to Vitez because he could not make a phone call from Zenica. But he came to me to Vitez to make his phone call, and he reminded me the other day that that is what we did on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So nobody -- there were no indications, there were no -- nothing that would perhaps indicate that it was a critical day, that the next day something would happen in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: No. In the evening, we watched television, as usual, and we then saw the story about the abduction of Zivko Totic and his escort in Zenica. But we had by that time already grown accustomed to those incidents and extraordinary situations because it had already become quite a frequent occurrence that the TO, that is, BH army, would be involved in some incidents directed at the HVO or individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that incident did not lead you to conclude that there would be a frontal clash.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: No, because incidents were a frequent occurrence and nobody could draw any conclusions from that, or at least I did not. I mean, I could not really draw any conclusions, and I think if anything important were happening, I would have learnt it, because such information always finds a channel to reach people. So that is why I think that nothing was in the offing, really, nothing was being prepared, because I simply did not have any information whatsoever about anything being under way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time that the defence office gave you any task? And what was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: I think it was on the fourth day, when the courier from the defence office, I believe he went from one door to the other, informing all the men of military age to report to the defence office. My building is not far from the post office building, and I went there straight away. I wouldn't know exactly the names of all those who were there. But a young man instructed me that I should go to the television building because he knew that I'd work for them, and he told me, "You go there because that's where you should work."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That young man from the defence office, did he first look at your mobilisation file in the office to see what was your earlier combat order, or what?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: No, no. I guess he knew something about me. It was just a couple of sentences that we exchanged when I reported, and then he told me, "Go and report to that team of yours, to that boss of yours, to the boss of the centre."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This television centre was where?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: The television centre was in the cinema building; that is, because of the misunderstanding with Mr. Pero Gudelj - I don't really know how and what - it was moved to the cinema, that is, the building of the Workers' University. That is what it was called before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It had been broadcasting its programme for some time from there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what area, roughly, that television centre could cover? What was its coverage?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: It was within, I should say, a diameter of some four kilometres, perhaps. And some villages could not really see it. I know they were trying to devise some technical solution, but it proved to be very difficult. So that was its range.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, I immediately became a journalist, writing stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That television, what role was it to serve? And you, as a journalist, what was it to serve?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: It was part of that information centre. I don't really know what the relationship was, but from the information centre, as a journalist, he would go out into the field and bring back information and there, I mean in the beginning, it was rather vague but, on the other hand, the role was to inform the population about the developments on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was also to boost the morale of the soldiers, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, in those early days, they needed no encouragement. Its role was to inform and to calm the situation, that is what the television was supposed to do. No propaganda, no -- that kind of encouragement of boosting the spirits. There was nothing of that in those early days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you perhaps explain why nothing was done in that regard in those early days; is there any reason for it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Because people thought that it was basically just an incident, just a clash which would be over in no time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But while we are on the subject and since you mentioned the building, the television station and its offices, they were not the only users of the premises in that building of the cinema or the Workers' University. There were also some other tenants, if I may call them that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: It is. Because I believe that it also housed the headquarters of the HDZ, presumably other parties earlier. At that time it was the HDZ, then the command was also housed there and I think a coffee shop. I don't really know, whether at that time it was still working or not. Whether it had shut down or not. Then there was the television. And I don't know if, on the other side, somebody also used that building. But yes, there were quite a number of users.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the command. What command did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: I meant the command of the Vitez Brigade, of the Viteska Brigade which had been formed sometime before that. I don't know really when they moved in, but they were there when I came to work there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And then at some point in time, you were sent, for the first time, as a soldier to the defence line. When was that and where were you sent?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Sometime in late May or perhaps early June, that even information workers were being asked to go to the defence line because they were short of men, the front line was being established, and we were called upon to go there to reinforce them and to do a shift on the front line. I think that was the first time that I went there for five days to the segment of the front line which is above Krizancevo Selo in the direction of the village of Tolovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zirdum, could we just clarify one point? Is it true that every adult citizen under the rules which were adopted by Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is the rules taken over from Yugoslavia, and under the rules also adopted by the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, every adult citizen in case of danger of war or imminent danger was under military obligation; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. Either military or labour obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that when you performed your work as a personnel manager in your factory, had to be familiar with those rules and all the duties arising from it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since you were familiar with the rules, is it true that in those first days when you were mobilised, you were placed on the labour duty or were you perceived as a soldier as of the beginning?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: I don't really know how they perceived me at the defence office. I simply accepted the duty. How they had it -- what they had on their official files, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you tell us that in those early days, you performed duties which were not military?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was in June that for the first time, you appear in a military capacity; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say you were sent somewhere to Krizancevo Selo, near Krizancevo Selo?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do there at those positions and how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: I was there with other four men from the television station or my fellow workers, we were five altogether, and we did guard shifts. As a matter of fact, there were two possibilities, the harder one on the front line itself and another one in a kind of a hollow where they sent novices. And when I came there, when I saw the two of my fellow workers didn't even know how to hold a rifle and they were terribly afraid, then I volunteered to go to the front line, that is to the hardest position, and let them go down to that creek or somewhere to stand guard there, not let anybody pass through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little before this, a week or two earlier, did you conduct an interview with refugees from Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, I toured the front lines outside Vitez because our television covered a broader area, there were no other media. And when the Croats from Zenica who were refugees arrived in the village of Grahovcici, I went to make a report about the refugees from Zenica. And it was already very difficult to reach Grahovcici so we went around the checkpoints where we could encounter Territorial Defence units. It was here that I conducted an interview with a witness of the massacre in the village of Miletici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These refugees that you mentioned from Zenica, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: They were Croats, Croats. It was civilians and soldiers all mixed up together, fleeing in chaos in the village of Grahovcici where the soldiers stayed behind, and the civilians were transported to the Lasva River Valley to Vitez, Nova Bila and Busovaca by a bus in very poor conditions and they had nothing but plastic bags in their hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you were then returned to your job as reporter at the television station after the position in Krizancevo Selo?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you sent to the front line again?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Around the 20th of July they called me up from the 3rd Battalion. They remembered that I had been a reserve officer in the former army so I was offered the duty of platoon commander on Crveno Brdce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you agree to this?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, what would have happened if you hadn't wanted to do that; could you have refused?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: At that moment, it would have been very hard to refuse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say "at that moment"?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Because the war was already raging, the situation was very complicated. There was a shortage of men, of professional staff, of weapons, and it was quite clear by then that there was a real conflict going on and that it could no longer be avoided. All hopes that this could come to a halt were dashed in the beginning of June when Travnik fell and large numbers of refugees started coming from the Travnik municipality to the Lasva River Valley. They came down the mountains and they were all driven down into the Lasva River Valley, and then there were no more illusions about this being a limited conflict. It was a real war in which we had to defend ourselves because we were surrounded on all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When you were sent to this area and took up these duties in Crveno Brdce, the Lasva River Valley was already completely surrounded?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any land route at that time to connect you with other parts of -- Croatian parts in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Crveno Brdce is, roughly speaking, in the area of Kruscica, not far from Vranjska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Until when will we be working so I know where to cut?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I hope you can finish this evidence. We started at twenty to, so we'll go on for another ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour, but I will not commit myself because there are some things that are going naturally here. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please tell me, Mr. Zirdum, what situation did you find when you arrived at your position in Crveno Brdce? I'm referring to the condition of the army, their equipment, organisation, and all the other elements of the army. What was your first impression when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: At Crveno Brdce, the defence line in the area where I arrived was running next to some houses. These were houses inhabited by the Krizanac families, several families called Krizanac. And the organisation was just beginning. It was hard for people to tell where they actually belonged in the establishment and what their title was. There was no well-developed system of defence with a clear vision of how to conduct the defence. Everything was at an initial stage. People were organising themselves ad hoc, and there was a lot of improvisation on that part of the line. I established a military organisation. I defined reserves. I said what should be done in what kind of situation and what in another, because the Muslim line was 176 metres away from our line, as the crow flies, in the central part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the line was -- that it ran past the houses. So you were facing the enemy and there was a Croatian village behind your backs?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, there were several houses which were on the line itself. There was even one on the other side of the line, and this was a problem I had to solve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From those positions in the sector where you moved at Crveno Brdce, can you see the minaret in Kruscica from any point?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, on the right-hand side of the platoon, you could have a good view of the minaret in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it there then?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was. It was about one kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see any damage to it? Was it possible to see any damage?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: No, we couldn't see any damage, nor did anyone from our positions shoot at it. We didn't have anything to shoot it with. And I would have punished anyone who wasted ammunition in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. How much time did you spend at that position?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: A little over a month. I don't know the exact dates, but I was there for a little over a month. When the line was set up properly, I reported to the commander that I had completed this task and that the people, the men there were brave, that they would defend themselves, that there was nothing else for me to do there, and could he give me another task because the people there were quite hard to deal with, complicated. I didn't want to remain there any longer. But I made use of my authority there for about a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then you were given another assignment.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that? Where was that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, that was in sector south, the southern side of Vitez, in the area of the village of Gacice, the broader area of Gacice, also a feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the hill of Osoj was where the front line was?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes. It's ten minutes on foot above the village of Gacice, to the left of the Princip company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That line or that defence position, did it play an important role in the defence of the factory?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes. It was a key elevation for the defence of the SPS company and the village of Gacice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived there, what kind of organisation did you find? What was the situation? What about weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, it was one of the worst and most confusing situations, most chaotic situations. There was no real line. The Muslims had not exerted much pressure either. It was high up in the mountain, on a hill -- they were high up on a hill from where they could have good control of the situation, and they did not have any need to exert a lot of pressure. So that was where our units took the longest time to organise themselves. Then I was asked to go and help the commander of that company to establish a better sort of defence because problems were expected from that side also, which proved to be true, because a day after I arrived, the Muslim forces attacked from that side as well and broke through at Bobasi, the Bobasi area, in the direction of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bobasi at that moment, tactically speaking, were your left flank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, it was the left -- the first left neighbour of the company I was in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the sake of those who are not there, Bobasi is just a little below Kruscica, in your direction?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: No. I was to the right on a hill, to give you the correct picture, in the direction of Princip, and that's more toward the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the area that you in the HVO, or rather in the brigade, saw as one of the possible routes that could relatively easily be taken by the army of BH in the direction of town?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, I was sent there to try to organise the defence in the best possible way, because we have the fewest men there and the fewest weapons, and the organisation was the worst there. We managed to organise defence when it was too late, unfortunately, because that was where the breakthrough at Bobasi happened. There was a big crack, a big break in our defence line. We were unable to close it because we did not have enough men. So we had to improvise our defence, and this resulted in the fact that we had to narrow down the circle in order to be able to close it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question about the details of that. On the first day when you arrived, according to what you were able to see then, did every soldier at that line have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: On the first day I managed to tour this position. I didn't have a chance to see the whole line in detail. But when the attack started, I did not have a rifle of my own, and when I went to see the men, they had old automatic rifles from World War II. There were two or three modern automatic weapons, up-to-date ones, and a few weapons produced in Croatia which happened to be there with very little ammunition. They were called Sokci in the local vernacular, and I took one of them home. It can shoot only at a distance of about 200 metres. It's a very poor sort of weapon. And I had one to stand the guard against the Muslims. Should I speak more about this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, there's no need to go into further detail. Is it true that you stayed in that area practically until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes, until the 1st of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that line you were formally appointed deputy commander of that company.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have another duty?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: Well, later I also became assistant for IPD, Information and Propaganda Department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you performed that duty?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For me, it is a good point to stop, and I guess that tomorrow morning I may have probably, I don't know, 15 minutes or so with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. How many more witnesses have you got this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We are hoping that we will have an additional two witnesses. They are, indeed, landing this evening at Schipol. Your Honour, we only got confirmation that they boarded the plane from Sarajevo at about lunchtime. I hope that both of them will be here this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I said earlier that we'd sit at 9.15. It doesn't seem necessary. We'll sit, in fact, at 9.30 unless that causes any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The registrar reminds me we were due to go on until 5.00, but we've made good progress and we won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirdum, would you be back, please, tomorrow morning at half past nine to continue your evidence. Would you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that includes members of the Defence team. Half past nine, please, tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
